## Topic summary
This topic teaches you how OneNote is organized and how to use it for class notes. You will learn the notebook structure, the five sections, and how to sync and collaborate safely.

## Learning goals
- Explain the OneNote hierarchy (notebook, section, page).
- Identify the five sections of the Computing notebook.
- Add content and tags to your notes.
- Check sync status and fix issues.
- Use shared spaces with good digital etiquette.

## Lesson 1.7.1: Understanding OneNote Structure
### Keywords
- OneNote: A digital notebook app.
- Notebook: The whole book.
- Section: A divider inside a notebook.
- Page: A single page for notes.
- Hierarchy: How items are organized in levels.

### Core content
Think of OneNote like a binder. The notebook is the binder, sections are dividers, and pages are sheets of paper. You can also create sub-pages under a main page to keep topics together.
This structure helps you keep notes organized and easy to find later.

### Key reminders
- Notebook > Section > Page.
- Use clear page titles so you can find work quickly.

### Try it
- Point to a notebook, a section, and a page in OneNote.
- Rename a page with a clear title.

### Quick check
1. What is a section in OneNote?
2. What is the full structure from biggest to smallest?
3. Why are page titles helpful?

### Did you know
OneNote was designed to feel like a real binder, but with unlimited pages.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing sections with pages.

### Exam tip
A section is a divider inside a notebook.

### Image briefs
- Diagram: Notebook > Section > Page > Sub-page.
- Screenshot: OneNote interface with levels labeled.

### SVG briefs
- Binder illustration mapping to OneNote parts.

### Interactive idea
Structure builder: drag items to make the correct hierarchy.

## Lesson 1.7.2: The Five Sections of Your Computing Notebook
### Keywords
- Curriculum Overview: Unit plans and outlines (read only).
- Learning Materials: Teacher notes and slides (read only).
- Assessment: Homework and tasks.
- Revision: Practice questions and review.
- Parental Information: Letters and updates for families.

### Core content
Your Computing notebook has five sections. Curriculum Overview shows the plan. Learning Materials holds teacher notes. Assessment is where you find homework tasks. Revision has practice questions. Parental Information is for family updates.
You should not edit teacher sections. Copy pages into your personal area before writing.

### Key reminders
- Do not edit teacher pages.
- Copy to your own section first.

### Try it
- Find the Assessment section and describe what is there.
- Copy a page to your personal section.

### Quick check
1. Where do you find homework tasks?
2. Which section is for practice questions?
3. Why should you copy before editing?

### Did you know
Teachers can see when you last edited a page, which helps them support you.

### Common pitfalls
- Writing directly in Learning Materials or Assessment.

### Exam tip
Homework tasks are in the Assessment section.

### Image briefs
- Screenshot: OneNote with five section tabs labeled.
- Table: section name, purpose, and student action.

### SVG briefs
- Five-tab divider illustration with icons.

### Interactive idea
Section matching game: match descriptions to section names.

## Lesson 1.7.3: Navigation and Adding Content
### Keywords
- Navigation pane: The left area showing sections and pages.
- Tag: A label like To Do or Important.
- Sub-page: A page nested under another page.
- Insert: A tab for adding pictures, files, or links.

### Core content
Click section tabs to switch sections. Use the page list to open pages. Click anywhere on a page to type.
Use the Insert tab to add images, files, or links. Tags help you mark important notes and questions. Sub-pages keep related notes together.

### Key reminders
- Tags help you review later.
- Use sub-pages to organize big topics.

### Try it
- Add a page and type a short note.
- Insert a picture or link.

### Quick check
1. Where do you add a picture?
2. What is the benefit of tags?
3. What is a sub-page?

### Did you know
OneNote can collect all tagged items into a summary page.

### Common pitfalls
- Not using tags, then losing important notes.

### Exam tip
Use the Insert tab to add files and images.

### Image briefs
- Screenshot: OneNote with navigation pane and Insert tab.
- Screenshot: tag menu with To Do and Important.

### SVG briefs
- Tag icons: checkbox, star, question mark.

### Interactive idea
Note taking simulator: add text, insert an image, apply a tag.

## Lesson 1.7.4: Sync Status and Troubleshooting
### Keywords
- Sync: Updating notes between device and cloud.
- Green check: Synced and safe to close.
- Red X: Sync error.
- Error: A problem that needs fixing.

### Core content
OneNote syncs your notes automatically. A green check means your work is safely synced. Spinning arrows mean it is still syncing. A red X means there is an error.
Do not close OneNote if syncing is still in progress. If you see a red X, tell your teacher.

### Key reminders
- Wait for the green check before closing.
- Report red X errors right away.

### Try it
- Find the sync status icon and describe what it means.
- Explain what you would do if you see a red X.

### Quick check
1. What does a green check mean?
2. What should you do if you see spinning arrows?
3. What does a red X mean?

### Did you know
OneNote lets you open your notes on any device with internet.

### Common pitfalls
- Closing OneNote before sync finishes.

### Exam tip
A red X means a sync error.

### Image briefs
- Screenshot: sync status icons in OneNote.
- Warning message: sync error alert.

### SVG briefs
- Status icons: green check, spinning arrows, red X.

### Interactive idea
Sync status monitor: wait for green check before closing.

## Lesson 1.7.5: Collaborative Spaces and Digital Etiquette
### Keywords
- Collaborative Space: Shared area where students can edit.
- Content Library: Teacher only area (view and copy).
- Digital etiquette: Respectful behavior online.

### Core content
The Collaborative Space is for group work and shared edits. Be careful and respectful. Do not delete other students' work.
The Content Library is read only. You can view and copy from it, but you should not edit it. Your personal section is your safe space for your own notes.

### Key reminders
- Do not edit the Content Library.
- Treat shared spaces with respect.

### Try it
- Identify which area is personal and which is shared.
- List two rules for collaborative work.

### Quick check
1. Where should you never edit?
2. What is the Collaborative Space used for?
3. Why is digital etiquette important?

### Did you know
OneNote keeps version history so teachers can restore deleted work.

### Common pitfalls
- Deleting other students' work.

### Exam tip
The Content Library is read only.

### Image briefs
- Screenshot: Collaborative Space with multiple cursors.
- Infographic: digital etiquette rules.

### SVG briefs

### Interactive idea
